title: Prevention and Resilience
description: Ten calm texts on how people and places prepare for hard times and recover from them: a town that makes room for floodwater, an emergency planner, the psychology of recovery, earthquake codes, airline safety culture, tsunami drills, a community garden, a near miss in a kitchen, nature's survivors and a grandmother's letter.

lessons.title: Making Room for Water
lessons.summary: A small town stops building higher walls against its river and gives the water places to go instead.
lessons.text:
Millbrook sits in a narrow valley in the northeastern corner of the state, where the hills are steep and the winters are long. For two centuries, the town treated its river the way one treats a difficult relative: with respect, with caution, and with walls. Each time the water rose, the town built the walls a little higher. Each time, the river found a way around them.

The change began at an ordinary council meeting. A young engineer named Ruth Alvarez stood up and showed a single chart. It compared the precipitation of the last thirty years with the precipitation of the thirty years before. The northeastern part of the state, she explained, was not simply getting more rain; it was getting its rain in heavier bursts, the kind of storm that drops a month of precipitation in two days. Walls designed for the old climate could no longer protect the town adequately, she said, and no wall could be built high enough to protect it adequately forever.

What she proposed instead was a new blueprint for the whole valley. The blueprint did not fight the water. It gave the water somewhere to go.

The first step was to look at the land itself. Upstream, farmers had cleared the trees along the banks long ago, and erosion had been carrying their soil into the river ever since. That erosion did double harm: the fields grew poorer, and the riverbed, filled with mud, held less water. Rain also washed fertilizer from the fields into the stream. The town offered to pay farmers to plant trees and grass along a strip beside the water. The roots held the soil, slowed the erosion, and caught much of the fertilizer before it reached the river.

The second step was in the town itself. Millbrook, like most towns, was covered in roofs, roads and parking lots, surfaces that let nothing through. On those surfaces, rain runs straight to the river in minutes. In soil, by contrast, it infiltrates slowly, and water that infiltrates the ground reaches the river hours later, if at all. So the town dug up an unused parking lot behind the old train station and turned it into a shallow park that floods on purpose. Two unused factory yards followed. On dry days, children play there. After a storm, the parks become muddy ponds for a day or two, and then they drain.

The Millbrook Gazette, the town's weekly paper, was doubtful at first. One editorial asked whether the council really meant to spend public money on muddy holes. Five years later, the same Gazette printed photographs of a storm that dropped more rain than the great flood of 1987. The river rose, the parks filled, and the main street stayed dry. The headline was only three words long: "The Mud Worked."

Questions:
What did Ruth Alvarez's chart show?
It showed that the northeastern part of the state was getting its rain in heavier bursts than before.
Why did erosion do double harm?
The fields grew poorer, and the riverbed, filled with mud, held less water.
What did the town do with the unused parking lot?
It turned the lot into a shallow park that floods on purpose.
How did the Millbrook Gazette change its view?
At first it called the parks muddy holes, but five years later it printed the headline "The Mud Worked."

lessons.title: The Planner Who Imagines the Worst
lessons.summary: A profile of a county emergency planner, a former waitress and forex trader who spends her Thursdays bowling.
lessons.text:
Dana Whitfield's office is on the fourth floor of the county building, and the first thing a visitor notices is the map: a large map of the county covered in small colored dots, each one marking a school, a hospital or a shelter. Whitfield is the county's emergency planner. Her job, as she puts it, is to imagine the worst event that is still plausible and then to make it a little less bad.

For ten years, she worked as a forex trader in Chicago, buying and selling currencies for a bank. Forex, she explains, is the market where the world exchanges one currency for another, and it never sleeps. "In forex you learn that the unlikely happens every week," she says. "You stop asking whether something is plausible and start asking what you will do when it happens anyway."

Before that, she worked her way through college as a waitress at a diner near her parents' house. A good waitress, she says, holds twelve orders in her head and stays polite when the kitchen runs out of eggs. "Every emergency is a crowded diner on a Saturday morning. Too many needs, not enough hands. What matters is whether you organized the kitchen in advance."

On a typical day, she might study how a hundred thousand commuters would leave the city if the main highway were closed. The commuters, she points out, would not wait for instructions; they would all try the same three side roads at once. Theoretically, the county has enough roads to move everyone. In practice, "theoretically" is the most dangerous word in her profession. "Theoretically, everything works," she says. "My job is the space between theoretically and Tuesday afternoon."

She also spends a surprising amount of time on hassle: the small obstacles that stop people from preparing. Asking families to keep three days of water at home sounds easy, but storing water is a hassle, and people avoid a hassle more readily than they avoid a risk. So her office now hands out free water containers at the county fair, already filled.

She is also responsible for the county's twelve shelters. To equip a shelter properly takes more than beds and bottled water: it means generators, medicine, toys for children and interpreters on call. Equipping all twelve took her four years.

Her colleagues commend her patience even more than her intelligence. The fire chief commends her in particular for listening to the people who will actually carry out a plan. "She asks the bus drivers before she asks the experts," he says.

On Thursday evenings, she leaves the map behind and becomes a bowler in a league at the lanes on Route 9. Bowling, she says, is calming: one lane, ten pins, and a clear result. "It's the only place in my week where I know exactly what is going to fall down."

Questions:
What is Dana Whitfield's job?
She is the county's emergency planner; she imagines the worst event that is still plausible and makes it a little less bad.
Why does she compare an emergency to a crowded diner?
Because in both there are too many needs and not enough hands.
How did her office remove the hassle of storing water?
It hands out free water containers at the county fair, already filled.
What does she do on Thursday evenings?
She becomes a bowler in a league at the lanes on Route 9.

lessons.title: What Bends Without Breaking
lessons.summary: An essay on what psychologists have learned about how ordinary people recover after hard times.
lessons.text:
For a long time, psychologists imagined the ability to recover from hard times as a rare gift, like a spring hidden inside a few lucky people that allowed them to return to their old shape. Research now paints a calmer and more hopeful picture. The ability to recover, it turns out, is ordinary. Most people who live through difficult events, such as the loss of a job or a serious illness, find their balance again within a year or two.

Some of the foundations are laid very early, perhaps even before birth. Studies suggest that long periods of stress in a mother's life can reach a child in the womb, shaping how strongly the body later reacts to danger. Yet the same research offers comfort: a child who was exposed to stress in the womb is not condemned to an anxious life. Warm, steady care in the first years can do a great deal to reset the system. Biology, in other words, is a beginning, not a sentence.

In adults, one of the most reliable signs of recovery is the ability to tell one's story without being trapped in it. A person may describe their woes in detail, but there is a difference between a woe that is remembered and a woe that is lived again every night. Psychologists sometimes speak of a transitional period, a stretch of months in which old routines have ended and new ones have not yet formed. The transitional period is uncomfortable, and it is easy to mistake it for failure. Usually it is simply the middle of the road.

Resentment deserves particular attention, because it often grows quietly in this middle stage. After a hard time, people may feel resentment toward a former employer, a relative who did not help, or even friends whose lives seem untouched. Resentment is understandable, but over the long run it is a heavy thing to carry. Many therapists treat it not as a moral fault but as a manifestation of pain that has not yet found another outlet. Seen as a manifestation rather than a verdict, resentment becomes easier to put down.

Recovery also looks different from place to place. What counts as healthy coping is culturally shaped. In some communities, people are expected to talk openly about grief; in others, the culturally accepted path is to grieve through shared work, such as cooking for a family that has lost someone.

Finally, some of the most useful tools are very simple. When worry tightens the chest, slow breathing helps: inhale through the nose for four counts, hold briefly, and breathe out for six. Inhale, and notice the shoulders; breathe out, and let them loosen. None of this removes a problem. It merely loosens the problem's grip long enough for a person to think clearly, which is often the first step back.

Questions:
What have researchers learned about recovery after hard times?
They have learned that the ability to recover is ordinary, and that most people find their balance again within a year or two.
What is a transitional period?
It is a stretch of months in which old routines have ended and new ones have not yet formed.
How do many therapists see resentment?
They see it as a manifestation of pain that has not yet found another outlet.
What breathing exercise does the essay describe?
Inhale through the nose for four counts, hold briefly, and breathe out for six, letting the shoulders loosen.

lessons.title: Steel That Gives a Little
lessons.summary: How earthquakes taught engineers to write stricter building codes and to design joints that bend instead of breaking.
lessons.text:
Deep beneath our feet lies the mantle, a thick layer of hot rock between the Earth's thin crust and its metal core. The mantle is solid, but over millions of years it flows, very slowly, like the thickest honey. The great plates of the crust ride on top of the mantle, and where they press against each other, stress builds until it is released in an earthquake. Engineers cannot stop the mantle from moving; what they can control is how buildings respond when the ground shakes.

For much of the twentieth century, the rules for construction varied widely from city to city. After several major earthquakes showed how dangerous this was, many countries adopted standardized building codes. A standardized code means that a school in a small village must be as strong as a school in the capital.

One lesson surprised engineers themselves. In 1994, an earthquake near Los Angeles damaged a multitude of steel frames in buildings that had been considered among the safest in the world. Inspectors found cracks in the joints where beams met columns. The problem lay in the welds. To weld two pieces of steel, a worker uses an electrode, a metal rod that carries a strong electric current and melts into the joint, joining the parts into one. Some of the electrodes used in those years produced welds that held firmly in normal conditions but cracked suddenly under violent shaking.

Researchers tested a multitude of new designs. They changed the type of electrode allowed for critical joints, required workers who weld those joints to pass special tests, and redesigned the connectors between beams and columns. The new connectors were meant to bend before they broke, so that a building would sway and absorb energy rather than snap. A weld, the engineers now said, must be not only strong but forgiving.

An Argentine engineer I spoke with, Lucía Ferrer, has spent her career on such details. She works in the city of Mendoza, near the Andes, where the Argentine government rewrote its own codes after an earthquake in 1977. Ferrer calls her country's code the magnum opus of her generation, the work it will be remembered for, even though it was written by committees and no single person signed it. "A magnum opus usually has an author," she said. "This one has thousands."

Not everyone welcomed the stricter rules at first. On her city's council, a bloc of developers argued that the codes would make housing too expensive. But opinions changed after the next earthquake, when buildings constructed under the new code stood firm while older ones needed costly repairs. The developers' bloc gradually became one of the code's defenders.

Questions:
What is the mantle?
It is a thick layer of hot rock between the Earth's thin crust and its metal core.
What does a standardized building code mean for a small village?
It means that a school in a small village must be as strong as a school in the capital.
What went wrong with some welds in 1994?
Some electrodes produced welds that cracked suddenly under violent shaking.
Why were the new connectors designed to bend?
So that a building would sway and absorb energy rather than snap.
Why did the developers' bloc change its mind?
After the next earthquake, buildings constructed under the new code stood firm, while older ones needed costly repairs.

lessons.title: No Captain Above the Checklist
lessons.summary: How airlines replaced the authority of the captain with a culture in which everyone speaks up and mistakes are reported.
lessons.text:
Air travel is now extremely safe, and that safety owes as much to a change in manners as to any change in machines. Until about 1980, the flight deck of a large passenger plane, where the pilots sit, was ruled by a simple principle: the supremacy of the captain. The captain was usually the oldest and most experienced pilot on board, and his word was final. A junior pilot who questioned him risked being thought disrespectful.

Investigators studying accidents of that era noticed a troubling pattern. In several cases, the recordings showed that a junior crew member had seen the danger. He had mentioned it into his headset, quietly, and then fallen silent when the captain did not respond. The problem was not a lack of knowledge on the flight deck. It was that the knowledge could not climb the ladder of rank.

The industry's answer was a new kind of training. Its central idea was that the supremacy of the captain should give way to the supremacy of the team. Junior pilots were taught to speak up clearly, and captains were taught to listen without treating a question as disrespectful. A first officer who says into her headset, "I'm not comfortable with this approach; I suggest we go around," is no longer being disrespectful. She is doing her job.

The same thinking spread to the cabin. Flight attendants, who in the early days of aviation were called stewards, were once seen mainly as hosts who served meals. Today they are trained safety professionals. A good steward of the cabin notices the passenger who looks pale, the bag that is blocking an exit, the smell that does not belong. When a nervous child is about to vomit in rough air, the attendant has a bag ready before anyone else realizes. Rough air that makes passengers vomit is rarely dangerous; a strange noise from the wing might be, so the attendant reports it to the pilots.

Perhaps the most important change was in how mistakes are reported. Many countries now run confidential reporting systems that work almost like an amnesty. A pilot who reports her own error, such as setting the wrong altitude, generally will not be punished for it, if the error was honest. Without that amnesty, fear would deter people from speaking, and the system would lose the very information it needs. Punishment, the reasoning goes, does not deter mistakes; it only deters people from admitting them.

On a long night flight, as one air traffic controller hands the plane to the next, the exchange is brief and polite. The controller gives a radio frequency and says, "Goodnight." The pilot repeats the frequency and answers, "Goodnight, and thank you." It is a small ritual, but it captures the spirit of the system: many people, each doing a modest part, none of them above the checklist.

Questions:
What was the old principle on the flight deck?
It was the supremacy of the captain, whose word was final.
What pattern did investigators notice?
A junior crew member had often seen the danger but fallen silent when the captain did not respond.
What does a good steward of the cabin notice?
The passenger who looks pale, the bag that is blocking an exit, and the smell that does not belong.
Why do confidential reporting systems work like an amnesty?
Because a pilot who reports her own honest error generally will not be punished, so fear does not deter people from speaking.

lessons.title: Reading the Sea
lessons.summary: How warning systems, neon signs and twice-yearly drills give coastal towns time to climb before a great wave arrives.
lessons.text:
On the open ocean, a tsunami is almost invisible. A ship far from shore might rise by less than a yard as the wave passes beneath it, a ripple so gentle that no one on deck would notice. The danger lies in the wavelength. An ordinary wind wave has a wavelength of perhaps a hundred yards, the distance from the top of one wave to the next. A tsunami can have a wavelength of more than a hundred miles. It is less a wave than a slow, enormous shift of the whole sea, and when it reaches shallow water near the coast, all that energy piles up.

Such waves differ greatly from typhoons, although both come from the sea. A typhoon announces itself days in advance: the sky grows dark, the wind rises, and satellites follow the storm across the Pacific. A tsunami may give no sign at all, or only a strange one, such as the sea drawing back from the beach. The water itself may change hue as the bottom of the bay is suddenly exposed, from deep blue to a pale, muddy green. People along some coasts have learned, over generations, that a sudden change of hue in the bay is a reason to climb.

Modern warning systems try to provide what nature does not: time. Instruments on the ocean floor sense the wave passing above them and send the readings to satellites. A ripple measured in the middle of the ocean becomes a warning sent to phones, radios and sirens along the coast.

But a warning is only as good as the response it produces, so coastal towns practice. In one fishing town, the drill is held twice a year. At a signal from the sirens, residents leave what they are doing and walk, not run, toward the hills. The aim is to evacuate the harbor district in fifteen minutes. Evacuating on foot is slower than driving, but cars would soon block the narrow streets. Bright neon signs, visible even at night, mark the routes. The neon arrows point up the hill at every corner.

The drill becomes a kind of procession. Teachers lead lines of students, and older residents are helped along by younger ones. The procession moves quietly up the slope to an open field. Many residents keep a pair of sneakers by the bed, because in a real emergency there may be no time to look for proper shoes.

Where there are no hills nearby, the town has built towers. Each one is a tall concrete structure with a wide outside staircase leading to a platform high above the street. The staircase is broad enough for two people to carry a wheelchair up it. Twice a year, the whole town climbs it together, and then walks back down to dinner.

Questions:
Why is a tsunami almost invisible on the open ocean?
A ship might rise by less than a yard as the wave passes, a ripple so gentle that no one would notice.
How does a typhoon differ from a tsunami?
A typhoon announces itself days in advance, while a tsunami may give no sign at all.
Why do many residents keep sneakers by the bed?
Because in a real emergency there may be no time to look for proper shoes.
Why do residents evacuate on foot?
Evacuating on foot is slower than driving, but cars would soon block the narrow streets.

lessons.title: The Garden at the End of the Street
lessons.summary: A retired man who moved to a new city finds company in a community garden that began with seeds thrown over a fence.
lessons.text:
When I retired and moved to a new city to be near my daughter, I discovered something that no one had warned me about: loneliness does not arrive with a crash. It arrives quietly, one empty afternoon at a time. My daughter worked long hours, and I could go three days without speaking to anyone except the man at the bakery.

At the end of my street there was an empty lot behind a tall fence. One spring morning I noticed that someone had thrown seeds over the fence. Within weeks, flowers were growing among the weeds. I later learned that this was guerrilla gardening: planting on neglected land without asking permission, quietly, the way a guerrilla army moves at night. The guerrilla gardener turned out to be a retired teacher named Marguerite, who had been an enthusiastic hippie in her youth. She still dressed like a hippie, in long skirts and beads.

Marguerite did not stay a guerrilla for long. She went to city hall, found the owner of the lot, and arranged a lease for one dollar a year. Then she knocked on doors, including mine.

That is how I came to spend every Saturday with people I would never otherwise have met. There was a young nurse who worked nights. And there was Yusuf, the imam of the small mosque on the corner, who brought a group of teenagers every week. The imam told me that a garden is a good teacher of patience, because you cannot argue with a pear tree. There were also Walt and Irene, who had both lived alone for years. They met that first summer, flirting gently over the tomatoes, and by the next spring the flirting had turned into a wedding.

The pear tree was the pride of the garden. It had been growing in the lot, half wild, long before any of us arrived. By the third summer it produced so many pears that we gave bags away to everyone who passed. Whatever we could not give away, we preserved. The nurse taught us to make pickles with vinegar, salt and garlic, and the imam's teenagers made a pear jam with apple vinegar and ginger.

The garden also has a funky little shed, painted purple and orange by the teenagers, with a hand-lettered sign that reads, "Take what you need." Inside are tools, seeds, and a box of goodies: cookies from the bakery and extra jars of pickles. A goody left in the box is usually gone by evening, and somebody always replaces it.

On cold mornings in spring, Marguerite brings a large jug of hot cocoa. We stand around the shed with our cups of cocoa and talk about nothing in particular, such as whose beans are doing best. Researchers say that loneliness can harm health as much as smoking. I know only that I now speak to someone every day, and that most of them ask about my beans.

Questions:
What is guerrilla gardening?
It is planting on neglected land without asking permission, quietly.
What did the imam say about the pear tree?
He said that a garden is a good teacher of patience, because you cannot argue with a pear tree.
What did the gardeners make with vinegar?
They made pickles with vinegar, salt and garlic, and a pear jam with apple vinegar and ginger.
What is inside the funky shed?
There are tools, seeds and a box of goodies.

lessons.title: The Dessert That Never Arrived
lessons.summary: A catering company catches a dangerous mistake at the last moment and studies the near miss instead of looking for someone to blame.
lessons.text:
Safety researchers like to describe a triangle. For every serious accident, the idea goes, there are dozens of minor injuries, and beneath those, hundreds of near misses: moments when something went wrong but, by good timing or good habits, nobody was hurt. Near misses are free lessons. An organization that studies them can fix a problem before it costs anything; an organization that ignores them is simply waiting to be unlucky.

Consider a small catering company in Portland, which I will call Bright Table. Like every catering business, it lives in constant fear of one thing: a guest with a severe food allergy receiving the wrong plate.

One afternoon, Bright Table was preparing a lunch for a law firm. One guest had a serious nut allergy, and her meal had been made separately and labeled. The trays were loaded onto a dolly, a small flat cart on wheels, to be rolled out to the van. As the driver pushed the dolly over the doorstep, it tipped. Bam! Two trays slid onto the floor. Nobody was hurt, but one of the trays held the special meal. In the rush, a cook rebuilt it using a dessert of pineapple and crushed nuts. The plate went back on the dolly with the same label as before.

The interception came at the last possible moment. The company had a rule that every special meal must be checked against its card by a second person before it leaves the building. The second person, a part-time worker named Hiro, noticed that the pineapple dessert looked different from the one in the photograph on the card. He opened it, saw the nuts, and stopped the van.

What happened next is what makes this a story about safety culture rather than luck. The owner did not ask who was to blame. She gathered the staff the next morning and asked how the system had allowed the mistake. The answers were practical. Special meals had no separate shelf, so they were rebuilt from whatever was nearby. Labels were attached to trays, not to the food. And the dolly had a loose wheel that had been annoying people for weeks. "I heard the bam," the driver admitted, "and I only thought about the mess."

Special meals are now packed in boxes of a different color. The dolly has a new wheel. Each card lists not only the forbidden ingredients but full nutritional information, including protein, fat and carbs, so that a wrong plate is easier to spot; a guest on a low-carb diet benefits from the same care. Hiro's interception is now part of the training, told to every new worker.

"We weren't lucky," the owner says. "Lucky would mean the guest got the right plate by chance. We were unlucky twice, first with the dolly and then with the dessert, and the system still caught it. That's the difference."

Questions:
What happened when the driver pushed the dolly over the doorstep?
It tipped, and two trays slid onto the floor.
How was the mistake caught?
Hiro checked the meal against its card and noticed that the pineapple dessert looked different from the photograph.
What does each card list now?
It lists the forbidden ingredients and full nutritional information, including protein, fat and carbs.
Why does the owner say they were not lucky?
Because they were unlucky twice, and the system still caught the mistake.

lessons.title: The Old Survivors
lessons.summary: Why crocodiles, small birds and coyotes have outlasted giants: a short essay on resilience in nature.
lessons.text:
About sixty-six million years ago, a meteor roughly six miles wide struck the Earth near what is now the coast of Mexico. The impact threw so much dust into the air that sunlight dimmed for years, and plants struggled to grow. Around three quarters of all species perished, including every large dinosaur. Biologists, however, increasingly ask a different question: not which creatures perished, but which did not.

The crocodile is one of the most famous answers. Crocodiles and their relatives lived alongside the dinosaurs, and they survived the meteor and the long, dark winter that followed. Its way of life protected it. A crocodile can go months without eating, it lives in rivers where food kept arriving, and it can slow its body down when times are hard.

Birds are another answer, and an amazingly dramatic one. Birds are, in fact, the last living dinosaurs, descended from small feathered relatives of the animals we picture when we hear the word. The modern raptor, whether eagle, hawk or falcon, shares more with those ancient hunters than its sharp eyes. The ancestors of today's birds were small enough to live on seeds, and seeds can wait in the soil through a long darkness. Amazingly, creatures the size of a pigeon outlived the giants. Watch a tall gray heron stalking fish in shallow water, slow and patient, and you are watching a very old way of hunting; dinosaurs were probably stalking their food in much the same way.

Some ancient animals carry clues in their colors. Fossil feathers occasionally preserve tiny structures that once held pigment, and by studying them, scientists have estimated the colors of animals that have been extinct for millions of years. One small dinosaur appears to have had a pattern of red and brown; another had shiny black feathers, like a crow. The pigment itself has long since disappeared, but the shapes that held it remain, amazingly, in the stone.

Resilience in nature is not only ancient. In North America, the coyote offers a modern example. Two hundred years ago, the coyote lived mainly on the western plains. Since then, while many species have struggled, coyotes have spread across the continent and into its cities. They eat almost anything, live in small family groups, and have grown accustomed to people in a way that wolves never did. In Chicago, researchers have followed coyotes that cross busy roads at night and rest in parks by day. The animals have become accustomed to traffic, to lights and to us, and many residents have become accustomed to them in return, often without ever seeing one.

The lesson biologists draw is the same in each case. The survivors were rarely the strongest. They were the flexible: the patient crocodile, the small bird, the coyote that eats what it finds.

Questions:
What happened after the meteor struck the Earth?
Dust dimmed the sunlight for years, and around three quarters of all species perished.
Why did the crocodile survive?
It can go months without eating, it lives in rivers where food kept arriving, and it can slow its body down.
How are raptors connected to dinosaurs?
Birds are the last living dinosaurs, and the modern raptor shares more with those ancient hunters than its sharp eyes.
How have scientists estimated the colors of extinct animals?
They have studied tiny structures in fossil feathers that once held pigment.
What have coyotes grown accustomed to?
They have grown accustomed to people, traffic and lights.

lessons.title: A Letter to My Granddaughter
lessons.summary: A grandmother writes to her granddaughter after a hard first term at college and sends her a handmade quilt.
lessons.text:
My dear Nora,

Your mother tells me that your first term has been harder than you expected, and that some nights you wonder whether you belong there at all. I am not going to tell you that everything will be fine, because my granddaughter is too clever to believe it. I am going to tell you a story instead, and then I am going to send you a package.

When I was 19, I left our farm to study music at a college that had once been a seminary. The old seminary still had its chapel, its long stone halls and its narrow windows, and the practice rooms had been made from the rooms where young priests used to sleep. I played the flute. I had been the best flute player in our county, which, I discovered in my first week, meant very little. The other students had studied with famous teachers. I had studied with the church choir director and the radio.

That first winter, I nearly went home. My money ran out in November, so I took a job as a cashier at a grocery store, working evenings after classes. Standing behind the counter, counting other people's change, I felt that I had failed at the one thing I had come to do.

What saved me was not talent. It was a small group of people. An older cashier named Mrs. Bell taught me to count faster and to laugh at difficult customers. A girl who played the piano down the hall asked me to play with her in the old chapel, where the sound was so beautiful that my mistakes seemed to float away. And in the spring, a quiet young man from my music theory class began walking me home from the store. He became my beau, as we said then, and later your grandfather. My beau, I should add, could not play a note on any instrument, but he listened to every concert as if it were the finest music on Earth.

Each year, on the anniversary of his death, I go to the remembrance service at our church and play the flute for him. It is a small remembrance, only a few minutes of music, but I find that remembrance is not sad when it is mostly gratitude.

The package contains two things. The first is a handmade quilt. I made it last winter from your grandfather's old shirts, so it is not elegant, but it is very comfy, and comfy is what you need at two in the morning before an exam. The second is a list of everything you have already survived. It is longer than you think.

Wrap yourself in the quilt and call me on Sunday.

With all my love,
Grandma

Questions:
Where did Grandma study music?
She studied at a college that had once been a seminary.
Why did she take a job as a cashier?
Her money ran out in November.
What does she do on the anniversary of her husband's death?
She goes to the remembrance service and plays the flute for him.
Why will the handmade quilt be good for her granddaughter?
It is very comfy, which is what she needs at two in the morning before an exam.
